Forecast a seasonal series with STL and a random walk with drift

Source: R/timeseries.R
ts_forecast.Rd

A dependency-free forecaster for a single seasonal series, which forecasts by decomposition (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021, Section 5.7). stats::stl() with s.window = "periodic" estimates a seasonal component that repeats unchanged in every cycle (Cleveland et al., 1990). The seasonally adjusted series, the data minus that component, is forecast with a random walk with drift, and the last cycle of the seasonal component is added back. The result reproduces forecast::stlf(x, method = "rwdrift", s.window = "periodic").

Usage

ts_forecast(x, h = 12, frequency = NULL, level = 0.95, lambda = NULL)

Arguments

x

A ts object, or a numeric vector (then frequency is required). It needs more than two full cycles of observations.

h

Forecast horizon: the number of future steps (a positive integer).

frequency

Number of observations per period; taken from x when it is a ts.

level

Prediction-interval coverage (a single number strictly between 0 and 1).

lambda

Optional Box-Cox transformation parameter. NULL, the default, forecasts the series as it is. 0 forecasts its logarithm, and any other number forecasts (x^lambda - 1) / lambda. Every observation must then be positive. The forecasts and limits are transformed back to the original scale, where the point forecast is the median of the forecast distribution, without the bias adjustment that would make it the mean (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021, Section 5.6). A forecast or limit beyond the range the transformation can reach comes back as 0 (for a positive lambda) or Inf (for a negative one).

Value

A data frame with one row per forecast step and columns time (the future times, on the same scale as stats::time()), fit, lwr and upr.

Details

The prediction interval at horizon h is fit +/- z * sigma_h, with z = qnorm((1 + level) / 2). The forecast standard deviation is that of a random walk with drift, sigma_h = sigma * sqrt(h * (1 + h / (T - 1))) (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021, Section 5.5), where sigma is the standard deviation of the steps of the seasonally adjusted series and T the length of the series. The band widens with the horizon, and the second term carries the uncertainty in the estimated drift.

The model assumes a seasonal pattern that adds to the level of the series and stays the same from cycle to cycle. When the seasonal swing grows with the level, as in AirPassengers, forecast on the log scale with lambda = 0. The band treats the seasonal component as known, so it leaves out the uncertainty in estimating it. In a rolling-origin backtest on five classic series whose seasonal swing does not grow with their level, the nominal 95% band covered 92% of one-step-ahead outcomes (dev/ts_forecast_backtest.R in the source repository). From three to 12 steps ahead, it covered 99%. The band therefore runs somewhat narrow at the shortest horizons and wide further out, where the uncertainty of a random walk keeps growing while these series stay close to their trend. For a different model, fit it with, for example, forecast::forecast() and pass its columns to timeseries_plot() as a data frame.

References

Cleveland RB, Cleveland WS, McRae JE, Terpenning I (1990). “STL: A seasonal-trend decomposition procedure based on loess.” Journal of Official Statistics, 6(1), 3–73.

Hyndman RJ, Athanasopoulos G (2021). Forecasting: Principles and practice, 3rd edition. OTexts, Melbourne, Australia. https://otexts.com/fpp3/.

See also

timeseries_plot(), decompose_plot()

Examples

# The seasonal swing of AirPassengers grows with the number of passengers,
# so it is forecast on the log scale.
fc <- ts_forecast(AirPassengers, h = 12, lambda = 0)
head(fc)
#>       time      fit      lwr      upr
#> 1 1961.000 440.0658 409.0407 473.4443
#> 2 1961.083 434.4320 391.6185 481.9261
#> 3 1961.167 499.4146 439.6286 567.3309
#> 4 1961.250 489.3344 422.1291 567.2391
#> 5 1961.333 493.5143 418.1409 582.4744
#> 6 1961.417 564.4599 470.4572 677.2453
# On that scale, the band widens with the horizon
diff(log(fc$upr) - log(fc$lwr)) > 0
#>  [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE
